blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the head of a **doubly linked list**, reverse it in place and return the new head. Every node's `next` and `prev` must be correct afterwards.

blocks.alt: Before: null, 1, 2, 3, null, with next arrows pointing right and prev arrows pointing left. After: the same nodes in the order 3, 2, 1. Each node's next and prev have simply swapped, and the old tail, 3, is the new head.

elements.text: in every node, prev and next have swapped
elements.originalText: in every node, prev and next have swapped

blocks.text: The idea: swap the two arrows in every node

Reversing a **singly** linked list needs three pointers (`prev`, `curr`, `next`) because each node only knows what comes after it. A doubly linked node already knows **both** neighbours, so reversing is even simpler: in every node, **swap `prev` and `next`**. The old tail ends up with `prev = null` — it's the new head — and the old head ends up with `next = null`.
The only care needed is moving on: after the swap, `curr.next` points **backward**, so save the old `next` before swapping and continue from it.
1. Brute force: copy the values and write them back reversed

blocks.code:
def reverse_dll(head):
    values = []
    curr = head
    while curr is not None:
        values.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    curr = head
    while curr is not None:
        curr.val = values.pop()          # write them back reversed
        curr = curr.next
    return head

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** It gives the right values, but it doesn't really reverse the list — the nodes stay where they were. Interviewers usually ask you to **relink** the nodes instead, which matters when the nodes carry more than a value or other code holds references to them.
2. Swap prev and next in every node

blocks.caption: Save next, swap the two arrows, move on — the last node handled becomes the head.

blocks.code:
def reverse_dll(head):
    curr, new_head = head, None
    while curr is not None:
        nxt = curr.next                  # save it before the swap
        curr.next, curr.prev = curr.prev, nxt   # swap the two pointers
        new_head = curr                  # the last node handled is the new head
        curr = nxt                       # move on (the old next)
    return new_head

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** One pass, and each node's own two pointers are all that change.

blocks.alt: Copy values back: O(n) time, O(n) space. Swap prev and next: O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: Compare it with **Reverse a Linked List** for singly lists: there, you rebuild the backward direction yourself; here it already exists, and reversing just means the two directions trade places.

items: **One node** — it is its own reverse; both pointers stay null.
**Two nodes** — the smallest case where the head and the tail change places.
**Moving with `curr = curr.next` after the swap** — that walks backward and stops at once. Use the saved next.
**Checking both directions** — after reversing, `a.next === b` must mean `b.prev === a` everywhere.
**Reverse a Linked List** (singly) — the three-pointer version, in the singly linked chapter.
**Reverse a doubly linked list in groups of k** — swap within each group, then join the groups' ends both ways.
**Is the doubly linked list a palindrome?** — walk inward from the head and the tail at once; no reversing needed at all.
